title: The importance of psychological safety: Amy Edmondson
transcript: One of the most important factors in delivering safe and effective care is psychological safety. Allow me to define that as a belief that the workplace is safe for speaking up, with ideas, questions, concerns and even mistakes. It's a sense of confidence that your voice is valued. You can think of this as a sense of permission for candour, that the workplace is somewhere we count on your voice being heard because you never know when you will have had the observation that someone else missed that will be mission critical to delivering safe, high-quality care. Now, I want to be clear that psychological safety is not about being 'nice'. It's not about holding back on something you think might be unpleasant, in fact quite the opposite. It's about candour. It's also of course not freedom from conflict. When you're in a psychologically safe workplace, there will be conflict. People will have different points of view and will get into it and will seek to understand each others views better and will come out with a better solution. Psychological safety in a psychologically safe workplace doesn't mean that all of your ideas will be applauded. It's certainly not permission to slack off, it's not a licence to whine, it's not oversharing - we still want people to be thoughtful and considerate in sharing work-relevant content. It's important to mention that psychological safety isn't the goal. Psychological safety is the means to the goal and that goal is excellence. That goal is commitment to high-quality care. So, it's important to recognise that for really high-quality care you need not just psychological safety, you also need urgency and commitment to excellence. If you don't have either psychological safety or a commitment to excellence, then you are working in what I call the 'apathy zone' where your heart isn't in it, you don't much like your colleagues and you're just not giving the work what you could give it. Certainly, if all you had was psychological safety and no commitment to excellence, then you'd be in what we call the 'comfort zone' where it's quite a relaxed state of affairs. I know that's not characterising care delivery today however this is the one that worries me. When your commitment to excellence and your sense of urgency are high but psychological safety is low, I call that the 'interpersonal anxiety zone' where your commitment to excellence is thwarted by not feeling that your voice is welcome. So, finally if you have both psychological safety and a commitment to excellence, that's the 'learning zone', that's the high-performing zone, that's where problems get solved, day in, day out, especially in health care delivery.

title: Amy Edmondson on Leading Up & Creating Psychological Safety
transcript: if you're not the boss or you're not the team leader many people think well there's nothing i can do i have to wait for the leader to do something and the truth is leaders do have an outsized influence on the psychological safety of a team or an organization but you have to distinguish between leader which is a role and leadership which is a behavior and leadership is the behavior that influence others in positive ways but turns out that any one of us can exercise leadership at any point the kind of leadership that you can exercise as merely a team member to make a difference in your team is quite profound and it turns out the same things that i recommend leaders do are things that you can do frame the work you can actually remind your colleagues that we're up against an incredibly challenging unfamiliar unknown path ahead and everybody's voice might matter like you can say things like that you can call attention to uncertainty to interdependence and that helps other people understand that their participation matters second anyone can exercise leadership on a team by asking good questions of their colleagues even if they're even of their leaders just ask questions every single time you ask a thoughtful question of a colleague you are giving that person a gift the gift of your interest the gift of your respect because you are implicitly saying i think you have something to contribute here any one of us can do that and of course responding productively is something you can do as well on a team someone suggests an idea you can say hey that's interesting i'd like to learn more wow you just made it more psychological say more psychologically safe and you advance the conversation at the same time
